summary:
## Game Objective
The goal of **Gin Rummy** is to be the first player to reach **100 points**. Points are scored over several hands by forming cards into groups called **melds** and minimizing ungrouped cards, known as **Deadwood**.

## Key Terms
*   **Meld:** A group of cards. Melds are kept in your hand until the end of a round.
    *   **Set:** Three or four cards of the same rank (e.g., three Jacks).
    *   **Run:** Three or more cards of the same suit in sequential order (e.g., 5, 6, 7 of Clubs).
*   **Deadwood:** Cards in your hand that are not part of a meld.
*   **Knocking:** The action of ending a round when your Deadwood point value is 10 or less.

> [!NOTE]
> In Gin Rummy, the **Ace is always low**. A run of Queen-King-Ace is not valid.

## Game Setup
1.  **Players:** 2
2.  **Deck:** Standard 52-card deck.
3.  **Dealing:** Each player receives **10 cards**.
4.  **Piles:** The remaining deck forms the **stock pile** (face down). The top card is turned over to start the **discard pile** (face up).

## Gameplay
Each turn consists of two actions:
1.  **Draw:** Take either the top card from the face-up **discard pile** or the top card from the face-down **stock pile**.
2.  **Discard:** Place one card from your hand face-up onto the discard pile.

> [!TIP]
> **First Turn Special Rule:** The non-dealer may take the first face-up card. If they pass, the dealer may take it. If both pass, the non-dealer begins the game by drawing from the stock pile.

## Ending a Round
A round can end in one of three ways:
1.  **Knocking:** A player can choose to knock at the end of their turn if their Deadwood points total 10 or less. They discard their final card face down to signal this.
2.  **Going Gin:** A player knocks with **zero Deadwood**. This results in bonus points.
3.  **Stock Pile Runs Out:** If only two cards are left in the stock pile and the last player to draw does not knock, the hand is a draw and no points are awarded.

## Scoring
Points are calculated based on the loser's remaining **Deadwood**, not the melds.

### Card Values for Deadwood
*   **Ace:** 1 point
*   **Number Cards (2-10):** Face value
*   **Face Cards (J, Q, K):** 10 points each

### Scoring Scenarios
*   **Going Gin:** The player who goes Gin scores points equal to their opponent's total Deadwood **plus a 20-point bonus**.
*   **Standard Knock:** If the knocker's Deadwood count is lower than their opponent's (after the opponent lays off cards), the knocker scores the **difference** between the two Deadwood totals.
    > The non-knocking player gets to **lay off** any of their Deadwood cards that can extend the knocker's existing melds. This can reduce their Deadwood total. Laying off is not allowed if the knocker went Gin.
*   **Undercut:** If the knocker's Deadwood count is equal to or higher than the opponent's (after the opponent lays off), the knocker has been **undercut**.
    > [!IMPORTANT]
    > In an undercut, the **opponent** scores the difference in Deadwood points **plus a 10-point bonus**. Be careful when you choose to knock!

## Introduction: The Goal of Gin Rummy

Hi! I'm gonna explain the crap out of that game. You don't know how to play Gin Rummy? Don't worry, I gotcha. Come on, let's go.

Hello. You'll often see Gin Rummy appear in old movies and TV shows, and that's because in the 1940s and '50s, this game was a national craze. Everyone was playing it, and it's still popular today. I think that's because Gin is very easy to learn, but if you practice, there's room for you to get really good.

There are many types of Rummy games because Rummy is a family of card games. This is a two-player game. If you have more players, check out my video on Rummy 500. Gin Rummy is played over several hands, and you'll earn points at the end of each hand with the goal of reaching 100 points.

In all Rummy games, you try to create groups of cards called melds. Any card not grouped in a meld is called Deadwood. There are two kinds of melds. There is a set, which is three or four cards of the same type. For example, three Jacks make a set. Four Eights make a set. The other type of meld is called a run. A run is three or more cards of the same suit that are in sequential order. Ace is always low. For example, Ace-2-3 of diamonds, that makes a run. Queen-King-Ace, not a run, because Ace is always low. Runs can be as long as you can make them.

One thing that makes Gin different than other Rummy games is that you'll hold all your melds and Deadwood in your hand until the end of the round. As you play, try to improve your hand so that you have the least amount of Deadwood possible. I'll talk more about scoring at the end. Now let's break it down how to play Gin.

## How to Set Up the Game

First, we'll set it up. You'll need a 52-card deck and a pen and paper to keep score. Each player draws a card from the deck and the lowest card deals. First, after that, my house rule is to take turns dealing. The dealer shuffles the cards and the other player cuts them. Deal out ten cards each and then place a card face up to form the discard pile. Place the deck next to the discard pile and that becomes the stock. That's it! You did it. You're all set up to play Gin.

## How to Play: Turns and a Special First Turn Rule

Now let's start playing. Each turn has two parts. First, the player draws a card, and then they discard a card. When drawing a card, they get to choose to either take the top card of the discard pile or the top card of the stockpile. After drawing a card, choose one card and discard it face-up onto the discard pile. You want to keep cards that you'll be able to meld and get rid of your Deadwood. And then it's the next person's turn, and they'll take a turn the same way. You just go back and forth just like that.

But there's a special rule for the very first turn of the game. So let's go back. Whoop! For the first turn after the cards are dealt, the player that did not deal has the option to take the first card of the discard pile. If they don't want it, they pass. And then the dealer has the option to take it. If either player took the card, then they complete their turn by discarding, and then it's the next person's turn as normal. But if neither player wants it, then the person that did not deal starts the game by drawing from the stockpile. Players continue drawing and discarding back and forth until the round ends. If a player has less than 10 points of Deadwood at the end of their turn, they can choose to end the round.

## Ending a Round: Knocking & Going Gin

That's called knocking. They just discard their last card face-down on the discard pile and knock on the table to signify the end of the round. A player could even knock on the very first turn if their deal was good enough, as long as they have less than 10 points of Deadwood.

But they don't have to knock if they don't want to. They can choose to continue playing to improve their hand. If they manage to have zero Deadwood when they knock, that's called 'going Gin', and they get bonus points. I'm about to talk about scoring...

## Ending a Round Without a Winner

...but first, let me tell you another way the hand can end. It's rare, but if you get to a point where there are only two cards left in the stock, and the person that drew the third-to-last card discards without knocking, the hand is over. Nobody gets any points. Womp womp. The dealer shuffles the cards and they'll start over with a new hand. Which alright...

## Scoring, Part 1: Card Values & Scoring a Gin Hand

Now it's time to figure out the score. What's interesting is that you do not count the value of the melded cards. The winner of the round gets points based on the amount of Deadwood left in their opponent's hand. Each card has a point value equal to their number. Ace is always one point, twos are worth two points, threes are three points, and so on. The face cards—Jack, Queen, and King—are all worth ten points each.

So if a player knocked, there are three possibilities: they win the hand by going Gin, they knock and win the hand by having less Deadwood, or they knocked and end up losing because they had more Deadwood. Let's look at an example of each. Going Gin is the best, I'll show you that first. That means knocking with zero Deadwood. If a player goes Gin, they get the value of all their opponent's Deadwood and also 20 bonus points. So here, that's 8 plus the 20 bonus, that equals 28 points. Write that down.

## Scoring, Part 2: A Standard Knock and Laying Off

Okay, let's score another hand. Whoop. If someone knocks without going Gin, they lay out all their cards. They separate their cards between their Deadwood and their melded sets. Now, the person that did not knock does the same, but they also get to lay off. That means they can take their Deadwood and include it into the knocker's melds. They can add to their sets or continue their runs, but they cannot meld into their opponent's Deadwood.

To be extra clear, only the player that did not knock gets to lay off, and they only get to do it if the knocker did not go Gin. All right, so after the cards are laid off, compare the value of the two players' remaining Deadwood and see who has less. Lower is better. If the player that knocked has less than their opponent, they win the round and earn points equal to the difference between the two counts. So here, the player that knocked has eight points of Deadwood. Face cards count as ten, so the other player has 22. So that's 22 minus 8, the player that knocked earns 14 points.

## Scoring, Part 3: The Undercut Rule

Okay, last thing. If a player knocks and ends up having more Deadwood, that's called being undercut. Let's take a look. Whoop. Okay, here the player knocks. The other player gets to lay off their cards. The player that knocked has 9, the other player has one and wins the round. The knocker's opponent scores the difference and also gets 10 bonus points. So here, 9 minus 1 is 8. Add the 10-point undercut bonus and the knocker's opponent gets 18 points.

So be careful how you knock, people! You continue playing hands and keep a running tally of your score. If you're the first person to win 100 points, that means you've won at Gin Rummy. Congratulations!

## Conclusion

Now you know how to play Gin. I touched on it at the beginning, but I wanted to talk more about the cultural significance of Gin. So as an extra bonus, I created a separate video with my top three scenes of Gin Rummy in TV and film. If you're interested in old-timey movies, well, I have it up on my channel now.

All right, everyone. Now it's time for you to decide if there's any buttons you want to hit. Did you like this? Did I present the rules clearly? Your comments and game requests are very welcome.
